claim: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is the largest cellular compartment.
source: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the largest cellular compartment, harbours the machinery for the biogenesis of secretory proteins and lipids, calcium storage/mobilisation, and detoxification.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the ER.

claim: The ER harbours machinery for biogenesis of secretory proteins and lipids.
source: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the largest cellular compartment, harbours the machinery for the biogenesis of secretory proteins and lipids, calcium storage/mobilisation, and detoxification.
evidence: Direct statement about ER function in the abstract.

claim: The ER is responsible for calcium storage and mobilisation.
source: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the largest cellular compartment, harbours the machinery for the biogenesis of secretory proteins and lipids, calcium storage/mobilisation, and detoxification.
evidence: Direct statement about ER function in the abstract.

claim: The ER is shaped as layered membranous sheets interconnected with a network of tubules extending throughout the cell.
source: It is shaped as layered membranous sheets interconnected with a network of tubules extending throughout the cell.
evidence: Direct description of ER morphology in the abstract.

claim: Mutations in ER morphogen genes cause neuro-pathologies.
source: Understanding the influence of the ER morphology dynamics on molecular transport may offer clues to rationalising neuro-pathologies caused by ER morphogen mutations.
evidence: Direct statement linking ER morphogen mutations to neuro-pathologies.

claim: Intra-luminal transport in the ER may be enabled by active contractions of ER tubules.
source: It has been recently proposed that intra-luminal transport may be enabled by active contractions of ER tubules.
evidence: Direct statement of a hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Reproducing transport with velocities similar to experimental measurements would require unrealistically high values of tubule contraction site length and rate.
source: The results of the model indicate that reproducing transport with velocities similar to those reported experimentally in single-particle tracking would require unrealistically high values of tubule contraction site length and rate.
evidence: This is a key finding from the computational model presented in the abstract.

claim: Width contractions of the ER's perinuclear sheets generate local flows with only a short-range effect on luminal transport.
source: Considering further nanofluidic scenarios, we show that width contractions of the ER's flat domains (perinuclear sheets) generate local flows with only a short-range effect on luminal transport.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model in the abstract.

claim: Only contractions of peripheral sheets can reproduce experimental measurements, provided they are able to contract fast enough.
source: Only contractions of peripheral sheets can reproduce experimental measurements, provided they are able to contract fast enough.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the modeling work stated in the abstract.

claim: The mammalian endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is the single largest intracellular structure.
source: The mammalian endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is the single largest intracellular structure (see sketch in Figure 1a).
evidence: Direct statement in the introduction with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: The ER is made up of membranous sheets interconnected with the nuclear envelope and branching out into a planar network of tubules extending throughout the cell periphery.
source: The organelle is made up of membranous sheets interconnected with the nuclear envelope and branching out into a planar network of tubules extending throughout the cell periphery (Figure 1b, Voeltz et al., 2002).
evidence: Direct description with citation and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The ER is responsible for the production, maturation, and quality-controlled folding of secretory and membrane proteins, which constitute approximately a third of the cell's proteome.
source: The ER is responsible for the production, maturation, and quality-controlled folding of secretory and membrane proteins, which constitute approximately a third of the cell's proteome (Ghaemmaghami et al., 2003).
evidence: Direct statement with citation supporting the proportion of proteome.

claim: The ER's membranes harbour the lipid biosynthesis machinery.
source: The organelle's membranes also harbour the lipid biosynthesis machinery, while its lumen stores calcium.
evidence: Direct statement about ER function.

claim: The ER lumen stores calcium.
source: The organelle's membranes also harbour the lipid biosynthesis machinery, while its lumen stores calcium.
evidence: Direct statement about ER function.

claim: The contiguous nature of the ER is believed to ensure an efficient delivery of components across the cell periphery.
source: The contiguous nature of the ER is believed to ensure an efficient delivery of all these components across the cell periphery.
evidence: Direct statement about the functional significance of ER continuity.

claim: ER luminal continuity and transport were demonstrated to kinetically limit calcium delivery for local release.
source: In particular, ER luminal continuity and transport were demonstrated to kinetically limit calcium delivery for local release (Crapart et al., 2024).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Mutations in genes involved in ER shaping cause neuronal diseases, including motor neuron degeneration of hereditary spastic paraplegia.
source: Such a link might help explain why mutations in genes involved in ER shaping cause neuronal diseases, including motor neuron degeneration of hereditary spastic paraplegia (Blackstone et al., 2011), sensory neuropathy (Kornak et al., 2014) and retinitis pigmentosa (Arno et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Mutations in genes involved in ER shaping cause sensory neuropathy.
source: Such a link might help explain why mutations in genes involved in ER shaping cause neuronal diseases, including motor neuron degeneration of hereditary spastic paraplegia (Blackstone et al., 2011), sensory neuropathy (Kornak et al., 2014) and retinitis pigmentosa (Arno et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Mutations in genes involved in ER shaping cause retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Such a link might help explain why mutations in genes involved in ER shaping cause neuronal diseases, including motor neuron degeneration of hereditary spastic paraplegia (Blackstone et al., 2011), sensory neuropathy (Kornak et al., 2014) and retinitis pigmentosa (Arno et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: The active nature of the ER luminal transport is suggested by the sensitivity of GFP bulk mobility to ATP depletion.
source: Empirically, the active nature of the ER luminal transport is suggested by a series of observations which include the sensitivity of Green fluorescent protein (GFP) bulk mobility (measured by Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and photoactivation) to ATP depletion (Nehls et al., 2000; Holcman et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Measurements of single-particle motion indicate inconsistencies with molecular diffusion.
source: Measurements of single-particle motion and chasing locally photoactivated luminal protein marker over distances, circumvent this limit and indicate inconsistencies with molecular diffusion (Konno et al., 2024).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Active flows in the ER may result from the stochastic contractility (pinching and unpinching) of ER tubules at specific locations along their lengths.
source: Based on ER marker velocity fluctuations measured in single-particle tracking and the detection of transient narrowing points in the tubules by improved super-resolution and electron microscopy (Holcman et al., 2018), it has been postulated that these active flows may result from the stochastic contractility (pinching and unpinching) of ER tubules at specific locations along their lengths (see sketch in Figure 1e); other plausible mechanisms for flow generation were also considered.
evidence: Direct statement of a hypothesis with citation and reference to Figure 1e.

claim: The tubular radius is estimated in the range 30–60 nm.
source: However, measurements for testing this pinching hypothesis are currently inaccessible, due to limitations in space–time resolution of live cell microscopy; the live cell-compatible super-resolution techniques achieve resolution of ∼80 nm at the relevant speed, while the tubular radius is estimated in the range 30–60 nm (Gao et al., 2019; Schroeder et al., 2019; Konno et al., 2024).
evidence: Direct statement with citations.

claim: The flow is driven by tubule contractions.
source: First, assuming that the flow is driven by tubule contractions (shown schematically in Figure 1e), we construct a physical and mathematical model of the ER network and solve it for the flows inside the network (description in Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct statement of a modeling assumption with reference to Figure 1e.

claim: The tubule pinching hypothesis is not supported by the results of the model.
source: We use our model to carry out numerical simulations to study the motion of Brownian particles carried by these flows and show that the tubule pinching hypothesis is not supported by the results of our model (Tubule contractility-driven ER luminal motion yields inadequate transport kinetics), a result independent of the network geometry (Tubule pinching-induced transport is network-geometry independent and fails to facilitate luminal homogenisation).
evidence: Direct statement of a key finding from the modeling work.

claim: The average flow speed in the C0 network is 1.3 µm/s.
source: The fluid flows in the edges of the network (model in Hydrodynamic modelling computed as detailed in Solving the hydrodynamic network model) reveal a rapid direction alternation of luminal currents (on average with a frequency of approximately 50Hz), as reflected in the changes of the axial velocity sign (Figure 2a), with an average flow speed of 1.3µm/s (see also Video 1).
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result with reference to Figure 2a and Video 1.

claim: Luminal currents alternate direction with a frequency of approximately 50 Hz.
source: The fluid flows in the edges of the network (model in Hydrodynamic modelling computed as detailed in Solving the hydrodynamic network model) reveal a rapid direction alternation of luminal currents (on average with a frequency of approximately 50Hz), as reflected in the changes of the axial velocity sign (Figure 2a), with an average flow speed of 1.3µm/s (see also Video 1).
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result with reference to Figure 2a and Video 1.

claim: The distribution of average edge traversal speeds from simulations (mean 4.4 µm/s) is lower than the experimentally measured speed distribution (mean 45 µm/s) by an order of magnitude.
source: Similarly, the distribution of average edge traversal speeds (defined precisely in Data processing: instantaneous speeds and average edge traversal speeds) from our simulations (mean 4.4µm/s, solid blue line in Figure 2c) is lower than the experimentally measured speed distribution (mean 45µm/s; Figure 2c, inset) by an order of magnitude.
evidence: Direct comparison of simulation results with experimental data, referencing Figure 2c.

claim: The results for all measures of transport under pure diffusion are virtually indistinguishable from those where the pinching-driven flows are included.
source: Moreover, the results for all measures of transport under pure diffusion, in the absence of pinching-induced flows, are virtually indistinguishable from those where the pinching-driven flows are included (see Figure 2b, c).
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result with reference to Figure 2b and 2c.

claim: Flows affect transport for Péclet numbers above order-one values.
source: Flows affect transport for Péclet numbers above order-one values (Leal, 2007), and therefore the pinching-driven flows have a negligible influence on the transport inside the ER network.
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: The pinching-driven flows have a negligible influence on the transport inside the ER network.
source: Flows affect transport for Péclet numbers above order-one values (Leal, 2007), and therefore the pinching-driven flows have a negligible influence on the transport inside the ER network.
evidence: Direct conclusion based on Péclet number analysis.

claim: Slip boundary conditions have virtually no effect on the average edge traversal speeds.
source: Our simulations show that slip boundary conditions have virtually no effect on the average edge traversal speeds (Figure 3a).
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result with reference to Figure 3a.

claim: A non-zero wall slip does change the shape of the flow profiles in the tubules but does not modify the cross-sectionally averaged flow speeds.
source: Physically, while a non-zero wall slip does change the shape of the flow profiles in the tubules (Figure 3b), it does not modify the cross-sectionally averaged flow speeds which directly affect global particle transport.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the physical effect with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: The distributions of the average edge traversal speeds appear insensitive to ER structure variations for both pinching-induced and exclusively diffusional transport.
source: The distributions of the average edge traversal speeds appear insensitive to ER structure variations for both pinching-induced and exclusively diffusional transport. This is reflected in the small deviations from the mean of the data points averaged across the different structures (Figure 2d, e).
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result with reference to Figure 2d and 2e.

claim: Pinching-induced flows inside a regular honeycomb network appear to be within a reasonable variance compared to the natural networks.
source: Furthermore, pinching-induced flows inside a regular honeycomb network (Figure 2f, inset) with a typical ER edge length (1 µm) appear to be within a reasonable variance compared to the natural networks.
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result with reference to Figure 2f.

claim: The presumed biological pinching parameters would be inadequate to facilitate ER luminal material exchange.
source: This indicates that the presumed biological pinching parameters would be inadequate to facilitate ER luminal material exchange.
evidence: Direct conclusion from the mixing simulations.

claim: The optimal sequence of motions to maximise advective particle displacement with two pinches results in a time-averaged displacement equal to the upper bound 8L/3.
source: We show in Materials and methods (Extension to nonlinear interactions between two pinches) that this is indeed the optimal two-pinch coordination, which results in a time-averaged displacement equal to the upper bound derived in Equation 1.
evidence: Direct statement of a mathematical result derived in the methods section.

claim: Junction volumes are drawn from a normal distribution N(0.0045 µm³, 0.0021 µm³).
source: We assume that the junction volumes are drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and SD as our data set that is the distribution N(0.0045 µm3, 0.0021 µm3).
evidence: Direct statement of a modeling assumption based on experimental estimates.

claim: The flow from perinuclear sheets decays sharply with distance away from the sheet.
source: Furthermore, our simulations reveal that the flow decays sharply with distance away from the sheet where it originated as it branches out into tubules. This is illustrated in Figure 8c, d and we further quantify the spatial gradient of the average edge traversal speeds across Cartesian 2D coordinates in Figure 8e, revealing the stark contrast between the homogeneous profile for contracting junctions (red dotted line) vs sheet-driven transport (blue solid line).
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result with reference to Figures 8c, 8d, and 8e.

claim: The short range of influence afforded by contracting perinuclear ER sheets argues against its ability to sustain mixing flows and fast particle transport on the distal tubular network.
source: The short range of influence afforded by contracting perinuclear ER sheets thus argues against its ability to sustain mixing flows and fast particle transport on the distal tubular network.
evidence: Direct conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: Peripheral sheets have volumes estimated at 0.12 µm³ ± 0.04 µm³.
source: The peripheral sheets have volumes significantly larger than tubules and junctions, which we estimated at 0.12 µm ± 0.04 µm3 (see Figure 13 and Materials and methods, Experimental estimates of volumes of peripheral sheets for details).
evidence: Direct statement of an experimental estimate with reference to Figure 13 and methods section.

claim: Peripheral sheet contractions may be offered as a plausible mechanism for fast luminal transport, provided they are able to contract with sufficiently high rates.
source: The contraction of peripheral sheets may thus be offered as a plausible mechanism for fast luminal transport, provided they are able to contract with sufficiently high rates.
evidence: Direct conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The energetic cost of one peripheral sheet contraction is estimated to be of the order of 1000 molecules of ATP.
source: Furthermore, by relating the work done by a peripheral sheet contraction to the dissipation due to the flows induced inside the sheet and in the rest of the network, the energetic cost of one such contraction may be estimated to be of the order of 1000 molecules of ATP (see Materials and methods, Energetic cost estimate for contracting peripheral sheets for details).
evidence: Direct statement of a calculation result with reference to methods section.

claim: A kinesin motor protein uses one molecule of ATP to move 8 nm.
source: For reference, a kinesin motor protein uses one molecule of ATP to move 8 nm (Coy et al., 1999; Schnitzer and Block, 1997), whereas a muscle fibre consumes hundreds of thousands of ATP per second (Barclay, 2017).
evidence: Direct statement with citations.

claim: A muscle fibre consumes hundreds of thousands of ATP per second.
source: For reference, a kinesin motor protein uses one molecule of ATP to move 8 nm (Coy et al., 1999; Schnitzer and Block, 1997), whereas a muscle fibre consumes hundreds of thousands of ATP per second (Barclay, 2017).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: The motion of solutes in cellular compartments is now understood to be facilitated by active components.
source: The motion of solutes in cellular compartments is now understood to be facilitated by active components. This is evident from direct motion measurements and the dependence of motion speed on the availability of ATP-contained energy (Dayel et al., 1999; Nehls et al., 2000; Holcman et al., 2018; Koslover et al., 2017).
evidence: Direct statement with citations.

claim: The cytoplasm's currents are often believed to originate from the motion of large complexes such as ribosomes and large vesicle cargo shuttled by cytoskeleton-mediated motorised transport.
source: The cytoplasm's currents are often believed to originate from the motion of large complexes such as ribosomes and large vesicle cargo shuttled by cytoskeleton-mediated motorised transport (Koslover et al., 2017).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: The contractility of tubules has been suggested as the flow generating mechanism in the ER.
source: In the case of enhanced transport in the lumen of the ER tubules, the contractility of tubules has been suggested as the flow generating mechanism, and indeed such tubule deformations have been observed in microscopy (Holcman et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Tubule deformations have been observed in microscopy.
source: In the case of enhanced transport in the lumen of the ER tubules, the contractility of tubules has been suggested as the flow generating mechanism, and indeed such tubule deformations have been observed in microscopy (Holcman et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Pinches with frequency and size on the order of those estimated by microscopy yield significantly lower speeds than single-particle tracking measurements.
source: The outcomes of our simulations for a contractile ER argue against the plausibility of local pinch-driven flow; pinches with frequency and size on the order of those estimated by microscopy yield significantly lower speeds than single-particle tracking measurements, as well as no enhancement of mixing beyond that from passive diffusion.
evidence: Direct statement of a key finding from the modeling work.

claim: Pinches with frequency and size on the order of those estimated by microscopy yield no enhancement of mixing beyond that from passive diffusion.
source: The outcomes of our simulations for a contractile ER argue against the plausibility of local pinch-driven flow; pinches with frequency and size on the order of those estimated by microscopy yield significantly lower speeds than single-particle tracking measurements, as well as no enhancement of mixing beyond that from passive diffusion.
evidence: Direct statement of a key finding from the modeling work.

claim: The deficit in transport stems from the fact that the displaced fluid volume upon local contraction is too small to generate sufficient particle transport.
source: The deficit stems from the fact that the displaced fluid volume upon local contraction is too small to generate sufficient particle transport.
evidence: Direct explanation of the mechanism underlying the modeling results.

claim: A combination of a higher frequency with a much larger pinch length may provide higher particle speeds that are comparable to the single-particle tracking measurements.
source: This sanctions exploring a wider range of spatiotemporal parameters in our simulations, which revealed that a combination of a higher frequency with a much larger pinch length may provide higher particle speeds that are comparable to the single-particle tracking measurements.
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result.

claim: The contraction of large-volume perinuclear sheets leads to fast transport but with a limited spatial range.
source: In contrast, the contraction of large-volume perinuclear sheets leads to fast transport but with a limited spatial range and with flows that would not impact transport beyond a few microns into the peripheral network.
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result.

claim: The alternative scenario of contractility of tubular junctions appears unlikely as particle speeds similar to experiments could only appear for junctions pinching at up to eight times faster than experimentally observed contracting tubules.
source: Similarly, the alternative scenario of contractility of tubular junctions appears unlikely as particle speeds similar to experiments could only appear for junctions pinching at up to eight times faster than experimentally observed contracting tubules.
evidence: Direct statement of a simulation result.

claim: Forces on the order of 30 pN would be required to periodically contract the tubules as seen empirically.
source: We have estimated in Estimate of forces required for pinches that forces on the order of 30 pN would be required to periodically contract the tubules as seen empirically.
evidence: Direct statement of a calculation result with reference to methods section.

claim: The force exerted by a single molecular motor has been estimated to be on the order of 6 pN.
source: The force exerted by a single molecular motor has been estimated to be on the order of 6 pN (Fisher and Kolomeisky, 1999), so the required forces for pinching may be provided by several motors working together (Jülicher et al., 1997).
evidence: Direct statement with citations.

claim: The required forces for pinching may be provided by several motors working together.
source: The force exerted by a single molecular motor has been estimated to be on the order of 6 pN (Fisher and Kolomeisky, 1999), so the required forces for pinching may be provided by several motors working together (Jülicher et al., 1997).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Recently discovered hydro-osmotic instabilities could contribute to shape fluctuations and pinching, although they are predicted to have much longer wavelengths than the typical size of a pinching region.
source: Recently discovered hydro-osmotic instabilities could also contribute to shape fluctuations and pinching, although they are predicted to have much longer wavelengths than the typical size of a pinching region (AlIzzi et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Mechanisms involving topological remodelling of the ER, such as ring closure, occur over timescales of minutes and cannot account for the millisecond-scale transport measured.
source: In contrast, the mechanisms involving topological remodelling of the ER, such as the well-documented process of ring closure (Guo et al., 2018), occur over timescales of minutes and therefore cannot account for the millisecond-scale transport measured here.
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Fluctuations in width of the flat ER areas are expected since the structures appear dynamic in live light microscopy and narrowing/extension points are observable in electron microscopy.
source: Fluctuations in width of the flat ER areas, in particular, are expected since the structures appear dynamic in live light microscopy and narrowing/extension points are observable in electron microscopy (Heinrich et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: Direct statement with citations.

claim: For structural fluctuation-based mechanisms to facilitate luminal motion, assumptions currently not supported by empirical data are required.
source: In conclusion, it is worth emphasising that our in silico fluid dynamical modelling reveals that for structural fluctuation-based mechanisms to facilitate luminal motion, assumptions currently not supported by empirical data are required.
evidence: Direct conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: The mean edge lengths in the C0-C4 networks are around 1 µm.
source: In Figure 9e, we show the distributions of the edge (tubule) lengths in each of the C0–C4 networks, as well as the mean edge lengths, the mean degrees (the degree of a node is the number of edges connected to it), and the number of nodes. The mean edge lengths are around 1 µm and mean degrees are approximately 3.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 9e.

claim: The mean degrees in the C0-C4 networks are approximately 3.
source: In Figure 9e, we show the distributions of the edge (tubule) lengths in each of the C0–C4 networks, as well as the mean edge lengths, the mean degrees (the degree of a node is the number of edges connected to it), and the number of nodes. The mean edge lengths are around 1 µm and mean degrees are approximately 3.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 9e.

claim: Junction volumes range between 0.0020 and 0.0081 µm³, with a mean of 0.045 µm³ and an SD of 0.0021 µm³.
source: Our new measurement of the intensities of the junctions then allows us to obtain estimates of their volumes; we obtain twelve values, ranging between 0.0020 and 0.0081 µm3, with a mean of 0.045 µm3 and an SD of 0.0021 µm3.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental measurements.

claim: The mean sheet volume is 0.12 µm³ with an SD of 0.04 µm³.
source: From our nine data values, we finally obtain a mean sheet volume of 0.12 µm3 and an SD of 0.04 µm3.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental measurements.

claim: The dominant energy expenditure in deforming a pinching tubule is in creating the large membrane curvatures at the narrowest sections of the pinch.
source: The dominant energy expenditure in deforming a pinching tubule is in creating the large membrane curvatures at the narrowest sections of the pinch, and much less work is done against the small volumes of fluid displaced (Estimate of forces required for pinches).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to methods section.

claim: The hydrodynamic contribution will dominate the energy expenditure budget for a contracting peripheral sheet.
source: A contracting peripheral sheet, however, displaces a relatively large volume of fluid without attaining the extreme curvatures required in a pinching tubule. We therefore expect, intuitively, that the hydrodynamic contribution will dominate the energy expenditure budget.
evidence: Direct statement of an expectation based on physical reasoning.
